extracted.intended_audience: biotech researchers, company inventors, university tech transfer offices, and patent practitioners seeking guidance on §101 eligibility and claim drafting for biotechnology inventions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what biotechnology subject matter is patent-eligible after the Myriad and Mayo Supreme Court decisions, and concrete claim-drafting strategies to survive §101 examination for genes, diagnostics, CRISPR, antibodies, stem cells, and related inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myriad: Genomic DNA is not patentable; cDNA is patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Genomic DNA (gDNA) is NOT patentable — even when isolated and purified from the human genome. Complementary DNA (cDNA) IS patentable — cDNA is synthetically created by reverse-transcribing mRNA and does not include introns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key test: is the claimed molecule meaningfully different in structure or function from what exists in nature? Examples: genomic DNA (isolated from body) ❌ not patentable; cDNA ✅ patentable. Synthetic genes (optimized codons) ✅; gene with inserted regulatory elements ✅. Avoid relying on 'isolation' alone — show synthetic origin or structural changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'markedly different from nature' standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-Myriad, a biotech invention is patent-eligible only if it has been meaningfully transformed or engineered beyond what exists naturally — i.e., is 'markedly different from nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For molecules, demonstrate structural differences (different sequence, different folding, different functional groups). For methods, show the process creates something or achieves a result that does not occur naturally. Mere isolation, purification, or discovery of a natural product or correlation is not enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo two-step test for diagnostic methods (§101/Alice framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Is the claim directed to a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea? Step 2: If yes, do the additional elements in the claim amount to 'significantly more' than the exception itself?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic claims often fail Step 2 because measurement and comparison steps are 'well-understood, routine, and conventional.' The framework was applied in Mayo and extended via Alice. Use this test to analyze diagnostic method claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements that can make diagnostic method claims survive Mayo
rubrics_metrics.description: To survive Mayo, diagnostic method claims should include elements that amount to 'significantly more' than a natural law or correlation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of survivable elements: a novel, non-obvious biomarker; an unconventional measurement technique that is not routine in the field; a treatment step that goes beyond merely observing and applying the natural correlation; specific clinical decision algorithms. Anti-pattern: claims that only observe a correlation and use routine lab steps are likely invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthetically created or engineered molecules are patentable when sufficiently different
rubrics_metrics.description: cDNA sequences, synthetic genes with optimized codons, engineered proteins with modified amino acid sequences, chimeric antibodies, and fusion proteins can be patent-eligible if they are not found in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize human engineering and provide sequence comparisons, structural data, and functional assays showing differences from natural counterparts. Claim both structure and functional consequences where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel compositions and formulations are patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Novel drug-antibody conjugates (ADCs), pharmaceutical formulations with improved properties, and nanoparticle delivery systems for biologics are examples of patent-eligible compositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to capture the inventive combination or improved properties (stability, bioavailability, delivery characteristics). Provide experimental support and examples in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genetically modified organisms (GMOs) and engineered organisms can be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Transgenic plants and animals with inserted genes conferring new traits, engineered microorganisms producing novel compounds or functions, and CRISPR-modified organisms can be patent-eligible when claimed to reflect human engineering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim the genetic modifications and their functional effects; careful claim drafting is needed to avoid §101 issues. Note licensing/ownership issues (e.g., CRISPR patent wars) may affect commercialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of making or using biotech products can be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Novel methods of producing recombinant proteins with improved yield or purity, gene therapy methods using engineered vectors, and cell culture techniques producing enhanced cell lines are potentially patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on technical improvements, unexpected results, and steps that are not merely conventional. Methods can provide a fallback if composition claims encounter §101 challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories facing §101 challenges: naturally occurring molecules
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturally occurring molecules—genomic DNA sequences, naturally occurring proteins/peptides/antibodies isolated from human or animal sources, and natural metabolites/biomarkers—face §101 patent-eligibility challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid claims that only isolate/purify naturally occurring items. To claim related subject matter, show structural or functional attributes that are engineered/novel versus naturally occurring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories facing §101 challenges: diagnostic correlations based on natural laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods claiming only the observation that biomarker X correlates with disease Y, or diagnostic methods using routine measurement techniques to apply a natural correlation, are vulnerable under Mayo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add concrete application steps (treatment decisions, novel measurement approaches, specific clinical algorithms) and demonstrate why steps are not 'well-understood, routine, and conventional.' Personalized medicine selection methods must themselves be novel and non-routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories facing §101 challenges: abstract data analysis and bare correlations
rubrics_metrics.description: Bioinformatics methods that merely analyze genetic data using conventional computational techniques, or claims directed to correlating genotype with phenotype without a concrete application, risk being abstract and non-patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus claims on particular applications, improvements in computer-implemented laboratory workflows, or inventive technical solutions rather than pure data analysis. Provide proof of technical effect where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: CRISPR-specific eligibility: engineered components and delivery systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to engineered CRISPR components (synthetic guide RNAs, modified Cas9 proteins), engineered CRISPR delivery systems (viral vectors, nanoparticles), and methods of using CRISPR to edit specific genes in specific cell types are patent-eligible; claims to the naturally occurring bacterial CRISPR system are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims around engineered sequences, protein modifications, delivery technologies, and specific applications. Be mindful of existing patent ownership and licensing needs (e.g., multiple groups hold patents with differing scopes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Antibodies and biologics: what is patentable vs challenging
rubrics_metrics.description: Humanized or chimeric antibodies, fully human monoclonal antibodies with specific binding characteristics, engineered antibody fragments, bispecific antibodies, and antibody-drug conjugates are patent-eligible; naturally occurring antibodies discovered in humans/animals are challenging under Myriad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize what makes the antibody structurally or functionally different from natural antibodies. Provide binding data, sequence/structure differences, engineered features, and therapeutic use evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stem cells and cell lines: patentable modifications vs natural origins
rubrics_metrics.description: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), differentiated cells produced through novel protocols, and genetically modified stem cell lines are patent-eligible; embryonic stem cell lines isolated directly without modification and methods using conventional techniques face eligibility challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim the reprogramming/modification steps and resulting functional differences. For methods, show that culturing or isolation steps are innovative and not merely routine, otherwise they may fail under Mayo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting strategy: emphasize structural differences in composition claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For composition of matter patents, the specification and claims should explicitly describe how the claimed molecule is structurally different from any naturally occurring counterpart and include supporting data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sequence comparisons, structural data, and functional assays demonstrating difference. Use precise claim language reciting engineered features and provide examples in the specification to counter §101 challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting strategy: avoid 'isolated' or 'purified' language alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-Myriad, claiming a molecule as merely 'isolated' or 'purified' is insufficient to confer patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must recite structural modifications, synthetic origin, or functional characteristics that do not exist in nature. Anti-pattern: relying on 'isolated from the body' wording without demonstrating marked differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting strategy: for diagnostics, add concrete application steps
rubrics_metrics.description: To survive Mayo, diagnostic method claims should include treatment steps, novel measurement techniques, or specific clinical decision algorithms that go beyond simply observing and applying a natural correlation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims that tie the biomarker measurement to a concrete, non-routine clinical action or an inventive measurement approach. Provide specification evidence of technical challenges overcome and clinical utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting strategy: use the specification to establish non-obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Mayo turns on whether additional claim elements are 'well-understood, routine, and conventional,' the specification should explain technical challenges, unexpected results, and why the claimed method was not obvious to skilled practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document experimental hurdles, comparative data, and unexpected benefits in the specification to support both §101 and non-obviousness arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting strategy: file both composition and method claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For engineered biologics, consider filing both composition claims (covering the molecule itself) and method claims (covering how it's made or used) because one claim type may survive when the other faces §101 challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use method claims as fallback territory and ensure methods include inventive steps beyond routine techniques. Coordinate claim scope to maximize protection while reducing §101 risk.
